title: Production AI Agent Platform
tagline: An observable research agent where every step is an event, every claim is checked, and consequential actions wait for a person.
stack: Python 3.12 · FastAPI · PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector · Redis (or in-memory) · SSE/WebSocket · MCP · pytest
evidence_line: 78 tests pass against a real embedded Postgres; live smoke run on 2026-11-01: 3 cited claims over 10 documents, groundedness 1.0.
problem: Most agent demos hide what the agent did, cannot show where an answer came from, and let side effects happen without a gate. The goal was a small platform where a run is a state machine, each step is a persisted event, retrieved text is treated as untrusted data, answers are verified against evidence, and a person approves anything consequential.
steps: A run is a state machine
Allowed transitions are a table; illegal ones raise. Every transition is an event, which makes runs debuggable and testable.
The model proposes a structured plan. It is validated (tool names, no cycles); a bad plan falls back to a safe single-retrieval plan instead of failing the run.
Vector and full-text search run together and are merged by rank fusion; passages that look like injected instructions are flagged and withheld from the writer.
A separate verifier checks citations and claim support, repairs once, then strips what is unsupported.
Consequential tools suspend the step until a person approves; a timeout means deny.
implementation: Run engine with an explicit transition table, per-run event sequence persisted before it is published, so streams replay losslessly after a reconnect.
Structured outputs validated with Pydantic; one repair round-trip with the validation error; otherwise a safe fallback.
Hybrid retrieval on one Postgres: pgvector HNSW and tsvector GIN, merged with reciprocal-rank fusion, plus a light coverage re-rank.
Tool registry with built-in tools and tools imported from external MCP servers; argument validation before execution; per-call timeout and retry.
Provider pool with a fallback chain; an offline deterministic provider makes the whole platform testable without a model.
decisions: Explicit state machine over a free-form agent loop
Resumable in principle, debuggable, testable, with clear failure classes. Cost: less flexible than a freeform loop.
Postgres for everything stateful, including vectors
One system to back up and reason about, with transactions across documents and chunks. Trade-off: a dedicated vector store would scale further.
Verification separate from generation, and again from evaluation
The online verifier and the offline evaluator are written independently so they do not share a blind spot.
Approvals are part of execution
Consequential tools suspend the step; decisions travel over pub/sub so any API replica can answer.
Retrieved text is untrusted
Injection patterns are flagged and withheld. The repository says plainly this is a mitigation, not a proof.
verification: smoke OK: run completed in 13 ms, 3 cited claims, 10 docs, groundedness 1.0
shot: The platform's operations UI, captured on 2026-11-01 from commit 7acb147. The badge reads "offline heuristic provider (not an LLM)".
Screenshot taken by me from the project running locally.
limits: The default provider is a deterministic, extractive heuristic, not a language model (the badge in the screenshot says so). Groundedness is high by construction and consistency is 1.0 because it is deterministic.
The evaluation dataset is a development set from the same author.
One process; the split into workers, tenant isolation and OpenTelemetry export are described as next steps, not built.
No hosted deployment is shown.
business: Operations teams need researched answers with sources and a gate before anything is saved or sent: supplier or policy research, report drafting, exception analysis. The pattern (events, verification, approvals) is what makes such a tool auditable.
source: project docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/DESIGN_DECISIONS.md; verification logs 2026-11-01

title: LLM Evaluation Framework
tagline: Turning quality guidelines into weighted, gated, repeatable measurements, with failures you can inspect.
stack: Python · FastAPI · pytest · optional OpenAI/Anthropic judge adapters
evidence_line: 33 tests pass; the bundled 18-case benchmark re-run on 2026-11-01 gives mean 0.6507 and pass rate 0.6111.
problem: 'Is the model output good?' is not a decision. Reviewers, engineers and policy owners need guidelines expressed as measurable criteria, with some criteria able to fail a case on their own, and a result that can gate a release.
steps: Criteria and weights live in JSON or YAML, so evaluation policy is data, editable and version-controlled without touching the engine.
Fourteen metrics (faithfulness, token-F1, ROUGE-L, BLEU, number match, schema validity, relevance, conciseness, refusal and safety gates) run offline with no keys.
Hard thresholds are separate from weights
A criterion can carry little weight yet still fail a case on its own, for example a safety gate.
A model can score a custom criterion through a plain chat(prompt) callable.
A result you can gate on
JSON, a self-contained interactive dashboard, and a CLI flag that fails a build under a threshold.
implementation: Registry of scoring functions that each return a value in [0, 1], so weighting and aggregation are uniform.
Rubrics loadable from JSON or YAML; evaluator applies weights and separate hard thresholds.
Self-contained HTML dashboard (no CDN) with filterable per-case breakdown; FastAPI endpoints and a CLI.
decisions: Deterministic core, optional intelligence
Heuristic metrics run in CI without keys; model judges are opt-in for nuanced dimensions.
Everything returns [0, 1]
Uniform scores make weighting comparable across dimensions.
Thresholds separate from weights
Safety and refusal behaviour can veto a case even when the weighted score is high.
Config over code
Policy changes are data changes.
verification: safety 1.00 · no_refusal 0.94 · number_accuracy 0.89 · conciseness 0.69 · faithfulness 0.67 · answer_f1 0.48 · relevance 0.45 · structure 0.41
shot: The dashboard produced by the benchmark run on 2026-11-01 (commit 99e6121): score by criterion and failing cases with their breakdowns.
Screenshot taken by me from the generated report.html.
limits: The benchmark scores a bundled sample set; the 61% pass rate measures the framework on that sample, not a live model.
Token-overlap metrics are not semantic truth; a passing benchmark does not prove broad reliability.
LLM-judge adapters were not exercised (they need API keys).
business: Anywhere AI output quality must become a repeatable decision: support answers, document assistants, extraction. The same structure (criteria, thresholds, per-category failures) is how quality standards are turned into a release gate.
source: project docs/architecture.md and README; verification logs 2026-11-01

run.where: README.md, installation and Quickstart, at commit 99e6121
run.note: Scores a bundled sample, not a live model.

title: MCP Weir: Governance for Agent Tool Calls
tagline: A gateway that decides what data may go where, given what the agent has already seen, with no model inside.
stack: Python · MCP over stdio · SQLite audit chain · pytest · hypothesis
evidence_line: 417 of 418 collected tests pass (1 skipped), including real subprocess tests; the built-in demo ran on 2026-11-01.
problem: Per-tool permissions say which tools an agent may call. They do not say which data may go where given what the agent has already read. A web page the agent summarises can carry an instruction to read a secret and e-mail it out.
steps: Results returned by tools are labelled by where they came from (for example, an untrusted web page).
Flow rules, not just tool rules
A read of a secret after untrusted content, or a send to an untrusted destination, is held or blocked by named rules (R-UNTRUSTED-READ, R-DEST-UNTRUSTED, R-FLOW-CONF, R-TRIFECTA).
Approvals bind to the exact call
A person approves one specific call once; changing it invalidates the approval.
A tool whose definition changes after approval is stopped (a 'rug pull').
Decisions are written to a hash-chained log that can render a flow trace.
implementation: MCP proxy between host and tool servers; deterministic rules engine with no model inside.
Session-level flow tracker linking earlier results to later arguments.
Approval store bound to call arguments; tool-definition pinning; tamper-evident audit chain; optional read-only local dashboard.
decisions: No model in the gateway
A control that a prompt can talk around is not a control. The gateway is plain code.
Information-flow rules over per-tool permissions
Action safety is not information-flow safety: a permitted read tool can still leak.
Same agent, three ways in the evaluation
Compare no gateway, a careful human, and an approve-everything human, so the rules are shown to hold even when the human fails.
verification: pytest (editable install; spawns subprocesses; 418 tests collected)
417 passed, 1 skipped (the headless-browser test, which needs Node and Playwright)

A no gateway: attacker got the secret · B behind Weir, careful human: read and send held, nothing reached the attacker · C behind Weir, human approves everything: send blocked by R-DEST-UNTRUSTED, R-FLOW-CONF, R-TRIFECTA
shot: The project's own read-only Control Center, flow view (screenshot from the project repository, commit 5df2745).
Screenshot from the project repository's documentation.
limits: A research prototype and a same-author evaluation on a synthetic world (invented mailbox, files and pages) with toy tools.
The demo is deterministic and uses no live model; the README's own evaluation used one small local model.

The README's 342 is the suite recorded at release time (2026-10-09, in the project's eval/results/tests.json). 76 Control Center tests were added after it, so the repository now collects 418; in the recorded 2026-11-01 run 417 passed and 1 was skipped (the headless-browser test, which needs Node and Playwright).
business: Any business that lets an AI assistant read documents and send messages needs a rule for what must never leave: customer data, credentials, contracts. This is a worked, tested example of enforcing that outside the model.
source: project README and docs; verification logs 2026-11-01

title: GenAI Document Assistant (RAG)
tagline: Grounded, cited answers from your own documents, with an evaluation harness and a reader that abstains when evidence is missing.
stack: Python · FastAPI · SSE · Docker · pgvector option · pytest (sister engine: rag-doc-qa, 14 tests)
evidence_line: 40 of 41 collected tests pass (1 optional embedding test skipped); the evaluation on 8 items gives hit rate 1.0, MRR 1.0, faithfulness 1.0, relevance 0.581.
problem: Document assistants that cannot cite, abstain or be scored cannot be trusted. The aim was a complete small system: ingestion, retrieval, a grounded reader with citations, a router for arithmetic, streaming, and an evaluation gated in CI.
steps: Sentence-aware overlapping chunks (about 480 characters) with a stateless hashing embedder, so everything runs offline.
Over-fetch by vector score, then blend with keyword overlap for better precision at k.
The extractive reader composes an answer from the retrieved sentences, attaches citations, and abstains when the context is insufficient.
Arithmetic goes to a restricted calculator rather than the model.
An evaluation harness reports hit rate, MRR, faithfulness and relevance with CI thresholds.
implementation: RAG pipeline: chunking, embeddings, vector store interface (in-memory, pgvector), retriever with re-ranking.
Router agent; reader behind one interface with extractive, Gemini and OpenAI backends.
Streaming responses over SSE; ingestion endpoint; Docker compose with Postgres/pgvector.
decisions: Extractive, abstaining reader as the default
Deterministic, offline, and incapable of inventing text outside the context.
Hashing embedder for the default path
Stateless and free to run; real embedders plug in behind the same interface.
Evaluation next to the code
Retrieval and answer quality are measured, not asserted.
verification: pytest (41 tests collected; the optional sentence-transformers package was not installed)
hit_rate 1.0 · mrr 1.0 · faithfulness 1.0 · relevance 0.581 on 8 items · EVAL PASSED (backends: hashing embedder, in-memory store)
shot: The chat interface (screenshot from the project repository's documentation, commit daba676).
Screenshot from the project repository's documentation.
limits: The 8-item evaluation set is tiny; perfect retrieval scores on it say little about arbitrary documents.
The verified run used hashing embeddings and the in-memory store; the pgvector path and real embedders were not exercised.
Relevance 0.58 is the weakest number and is reported as such.
The project README quotes older test counts (29 in the quick start, 39 in the file listing); the recorded run collected 41.
business: Teams with policy, menu, supplier or HR documents need answers with sources, and need to know when the system should say it does not know.

run.where: README.md, quick start (install lines) and the eval command it names, at commit daba676; the eval is run from backend/ as in the verification log

title: Support Escalation Copilot
tagline: An approval-gated agent workflow where the model proposes and deterministic code decides, with an audit trail and tenant isolation.
stack: Python 3.12 · PostgreSQL + pgvector (row-level security) · server-rendered operator UI · pytest
evidence_line: 489 tests pass (plus one documented expected failure) on a real embedded Postgres; 21 of 21 demo checks passed on 2026-11-01.
problem: An agent is useful for reading and reconciling messy evidence, and dangerous where the work is deciding who may do what. The question was how to let a model help with a support escalation while the things that can hurt a customer stay under deterministic control and human approval.
steps: The model works inside steps; it does not plan the workflow, choose the tenant, the approver or the workflow state.
Model output must pass schema, citation and grounding checks; a privileged field makes it invalid.
Deterministic rules over trusted facts decide whether an action is allowed.
Approvals bind to the action, role, tenant and expiry; amending the action requires a new approval.
If an external write may or may not have happened, the case is marked uncertain, not retried, and reconciled by a person.
implementation: Five typed actions (two propose-only, three human-gated); a vocabulary the model cannot extend.
PostgreSQL row-level security for tenant isolation; uniform 404 for foreign cases.
Idempotent execution, crash recovery with leases, and a hash-chained audit log that is verified in the demo.
decisions: Fixed workflow, not free-form planning
Predictable and testable; the model contributes reading and drafting, not control.
Deterministic policy engine
No model confidence or retrieval score is an input to an authorisation decision.
Do not retry uncertain writes
An unknown outcome is handed to a person instead of risking a duplicate.
verification: pytest with embedded Postgres (runtime installed from its pinned commit)

21/21 demo checks passed, including: prompt-injection contained · uncertain execution handed off, not retried · another tenant gets the same 404 for a real and a nonexistent case · audit trail verifies (hash chain)
shot: The approval panel shows the exact action to be approved (screenshot from the project repository's documentation).
Screenshot from the project repository's documentation.
limits: The default model is a rule-based stand-in, not an LLM; the repository reports one small real-model evaluation separately.
The scenario is a fictional B2B SaaS support team on synthetic data.
The tests require the pinned agent runtime from another repository (ai-agent-from-scratch).
business: Support, finance and operations escalations where an assistant may draft and recommend but a person must authorise anything that changes a customer's account.

title: NASHA AI Lab: Architecture and an Honest Evaluation
tagline: An evaluation-first design for AI in business operations, built around a proposed brewery and reported with its failures.
commit: not published (the public repository shows an earlier state)
stack: Python · FastAPI · PostgreSQL · pytest · independent scorer
evidence_line: 953 offline tests passed at a local review checkpoint that is not yet public; the live model evaluation has not passed.
problem: Can a language model explain an operations gap (for example, expected stock against counted stock) using only verified facts, abstain when the facts are missing or conflicting, and ignore text that tries to instruct it, and how would we know? NASHA, a proposed Indo-Mex brewery, is the business scenario. It is a concept: no customers, suppliers or revenue.
steps: The business facts are a trusted snapshot. Text such as an entity's alias is data, never an instruction.
The model's output is a structured set of claims. Nothing it writes is shown unless every claim verifies.
Each number, unit and fact reference is checked; abstention with exactly the right reasons is a correct answer.
What a person reads is rendered by code from the verified facts, not copied from the model.
Gates were written before the run
Acceptance thresholds, the 60-case set and an independent scorer were fixed in advance and are not changed after seeing results.
implementation: Validator and renderer with 60 official cases, a diagnostic set and an independent scorer.
Paired diagnostic experiment comparing two prompts on 21 pinned cases, implemented and tested offline (not yet run against a model).
Evidence handling with a hash-chained ledger, single-use approvals and secret scanning of exported evidence; these controls went through four rounds of independent AI-assisted review.
decisions: Pre-register the gates
Thresholds are not lowered to make a model pass.
Separate generation, validation and scoring
The scorer is independent of the code under test.
Publish the failure
A strict, failing evaluation with a clear cause is more useful than a demo with no evidence.
verification: Offline tests at a local review checkpoint (not yet public)
953 passed (evaluation harness and evidence controls); scripted end-to-end self-test passes (scripted evidence is never a result)
0 of 30 supported cases accepted; every attempt was cut off before finishing; the cause is unknown
three rejections, all explained by the prompt: a shortfall reported as -267 when the rule gives +267, an extra reason code, and an unnecessary abstention
limits: **Live evaluation not passed.** The model has not met its acceptance criteria.
A candidate prompt fix exists and has not been tested against a model; the paired GPU re-run is planned and has not been run.
Passing 953 offline tests shows the harness and controls behave as tested; it is not model capability or production readiness.
Not deployed; the brewery is a business concept, not an operating business; the review was AI-assisted, not a formal external audit.
business: Any operations team considering AI explanations (inventory, supplier, finance) needs the same discipline: define the contract, verify every claim against facts, measure honestly, and keep a person in the loop.
source: lab documentation and evaluation records; verification logs 2026-11-01
